extracted.intended_audience: students and professionals studying engineering ethics, product safety, and tort/regulatory law
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing product-safety decision-making and corporate ethics using the Ford Pinto case — focusing on risk-benefit calculations, negligence calculus, regulatory compliance, and professional duties of engineers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calculus of Negligence (Hand Rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The hand rule: if the probability of loss (P) multiplied by the magnitude of the loss (L) is higher than the burden (B) of taking precautions, then one is required to take those precautions (PL > B indicates duty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained as a legal standard for breach of duty with the precedent United States v. Carroll Towing Co. (1947) used as an example; used to evaluate whether costlier safety measures were legally required given probability and magnitude of harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use rigorous risk-benefit analysis (full disclosure of inputs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cost-benefit analyses must correctly weight harms avoided against costs of preventative measures; the Pinto 'memo' compared an $11-per-car fix to estimated costs of deaths/injuries and legal settlements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page shows how input choices (injury incidence, value of life, unit repair cost) change the conclusion; guidance implies analyses must use realistic, well-documented inputs and be transparent rather than concealed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate injury incidence realistically
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not equate incidence of burn injuries with burn deaths; Ford assumed injuries equaled deaths (180), while experts argued injuries would be far higher (roughly 10:1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using a tenfold higher injury estimate (1800) dramatically changes the cost-benefit outcome; analysts should use empirically justified injury-to-death ratios and sensitivity analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate/value-for-life figures from accepted sources
rubrics_metrics.description: The monetary valuation of human life is a central input in risk-benefit calculations; Ford used $200,000 while NHTSA suggested $275,000 and other federal agencies used $350,000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting a deliberately low life-value can skew analysis to favor non-action; guidance is to use accepted agency values or justify deviations and be transparent about ethical implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use realistic unit-repair costs and consider third-party solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Unit cost estimates for fixes must reflect feasible engineering remedies; Ford estimated $11 per vehicle while third-party proposals (e.g., Goodyear rubber bladder) could cost under $5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overstating repair costs inflates the apparent cost of safety; analyses should survey available technical fixes and cost them realistically rather than assuming a single high estimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish and disclose safety test results
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacturers should not withhold test results relevant to public safety; Ford continued production without publishing test results that showed fuel-tank puncture risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Withholding test data undermines public trust and prevents regulators and other manufacturers from assessing risk; transparency is a professional obligation according to the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comply with regulatory fuel-system standards (FMVSS 301)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fuel system integrity standards such as FMVSS 301 are intended to tighten safety requirements and may necessitate design changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes Ford lobbied to delay FMVSS 301 and delayed fixes until legally required; guidance implies manufacturers should design to meet or exceed such standards rather than work to postpone them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initiate recalls when defects are found
rubrics_metrics.description: When regulators or testing establish a defect (e.g., NHTSA concluded the Pinto fuel system was defective), manufacturers should carry out recalls and corrective modifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ford eventually issued a voluntary recall (over 1.5 million vehicles) and mandated shields and more resistant fuel tanks; the narrative supports prompt remedial action rather than waiting for legal compulsion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engineers' duty to public safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Engineers have a duty to create designs that greatly reduce risks of harm and to prioritize public safety over cost-cutting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical takeaway: professionals should ask 'Is this safe?' rather than 'What is this life worth?'; holding to a safety-focused professional code could have avoided many calamities in the Pinto case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid lobbying to delay safety regulations or fixes
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporate attempts to delay safety legislation (Ford's lobbying to postpone FMVSS 301) and to postpone design fixes until legally required are ethically problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page criticizes voting to delay fixes and lobbying that prevents regulatory standards from taking effect; guidance implies companies should not use influence to avoid implementing safety improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support and protect whistleblowing on safety issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Engineers and test personnel have an obligation to report serious safety inadequacies (example: Harley Copp, Ford test engineer, acting as a whistleblower).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encouraging and protecting internal reporting helps surface design defects earlier; the narrative presents whistleblowing as an important corrective mechanism when internal concerns are ignored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize potential criminal liability for reckless product decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies and managers may face criminal charges (e.g., reckless homicide/recklessness) in severe product-safety failures; Ford was once charged (charges later dropped) after rear-end fatalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond civil liability, organizations should be aware of criminal exposure for recklessness in product design or deliberate disregard for safety, which raises the stakes for ethical decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulators may use extreme/worst-case testing to justify recalls
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulators (NHTSA) sometimes employ extreme test parameters to maximize damage potential and demonstrate defects; such tests may cause many small cars to 'fail' by design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes NHTSA used worst-case testing and defended it as necessary; manufacturers should understand regulatory testing regimes and not dismiss extreme-test findings as irrelevant without substantive rebuttal.
